question: In Java, which of the following is a strict requirement for a subclass method to successfully override an instance method defined in its superclass?

options.text: The subclass method must include the @Override annotation, or the compiler will treat it as an unrelated method.
The subclass method must have the exact same method name and parameter list as the superclass method.
The subclass method must be declared with a more restrictive access modifier than the superclass method.
The subclass method can have a completely different parameter list as long as its return type is identical.

explanation: Method overriding requires the subclass method to have the exact same signature (name and parameter types) as the superclass method. The notion that visibility can be reduced is wrong because Java prohibits weaker access privileges. The claim that @Override is mandatory is incorrect because overriding occurs automatically when signatures match, and differing parameter lists define an overload rather than an override.

question: What happens if a subclass attempts to declare a method with the exact same signature as a final instance method in its superclass?

options.text: The subclass method overloads the final method, making both accessible depending on arguments.
The subclass method successfully overrides the superclass method at runtime.
A compile-time error occurs because final methods cannot be overridden.
The code compiles successfully but throws an UnsupportedOperationException when executed.

explanation: Marking an instance method as final explicitly prohibits subclasses from overriding it; any attempt to do so produces a compilation error. The claim that final methods can still be overridden ignores compiler enforcement of the final modifier. The suggestion that identical signatures overload confuses overriding with overloading.

options.text: Car
Compilation error because duplicate method names in subclasses must have different parameters to overload
Vehicle
Compilation error because @Override was omitted on the subclass method

explanation: Because start() is an overridden instance method, dynamic method dispatch invokes the implementation corresponding to the actual runtime object (Car), printing 'Car '. The output 'Vehicle ' falsely assumes reference type determines instance method dispatch. The claim that omitting @Override causes a compile error is false because overriding is valid without annotations.

options.text: Runtime error because SuperClass cannot hold an instance of SubClass.
No error; it compiles and prints "Sub".
Compile-time error because execute must return an int.
Compile-time error because SubClass cannot assign weaker access privileges (protected) than SuperClass (public).

explanation: An overriding method cannot reduce the visibility of the method it overrides. In SuperClass, execute() is public; in SubClass, declaring it protected reduces visibility, which violates subtyping rules and triggers a compilation error. The claim that it compiles without error overlooks access modifier restrictions on overriding.

options.text: Super Sub
Compilation error because static methods cannot share names in subclasses.
Super
Sub

explanation: Static methods are hidden rather than overridden. Invocations of static methods are bound at compile time based strictly on the declared reference type (SuperType), so 'Super ' is printed. The output 'Sub ' mistakenly presumes static methods participate in dynamic polymorphic dispatch.

options.text: Dog defines makeSound() with an incompatible return type (int instead of void) for overriding.
Subclasses are not allowed to override methods that have no parameters.
Animal cannot be instantiated because its method has a body.
Dog must use the @Override annotation to compile.

explanation: When overriding a method with the same parameter signature, the return type must be identical or covariant. Changing void to int is not a valid override and causes a compile-time clash. The assertion that parameterless methods cannot be overridden confuses overloading with overriding.

options.text: Compilation error because FastCalculator did not use @Override.

explanation: FastCalculator defines compute(double, int), which overloads rather than overrides compute(int, double). Since reference c is of declared type Calculator, calling compute(4, 2.0) resolves to Calculator's method at compile time, returning 4 + 2.0 = 6.0. The output 8.0 mistakenly treats reordered parameter types as an override.

question: Which statement correctly describes the role of the @Override annotation on a Java method?

options.text: It changes the dispatch mechanism of the method from static to dynamic.
It instructs the compiler to verify that the method actually overrides a declaration in a supertype.
It is mandatory; the JVM will ignore subclass overrides at runtime without it.
It enables the method to override final methods defined in parent classes.

explanation: The @Override annotation provides a compile-time check ensuring the annotated method properly overrides a superclass or interface declaration. If no matching supertype method exists, compilation fails. The belief that @Override is mandatory for overriding to work at runtime is incorrect, as dispatch is dynamic regardless of annotation presence.

options.text: ClassCastException at runtime when assigning Derived to Base.
Compile-time error because overriding methods must have the identical return type, not a subtype.

explanation: Java supports covariant return types: an overriding method can return a subtype (Integer) of the superclass method's return type (Number). At runtime, dynamic dispatch invokes Derived.getValue(), printing 20. Claiming that return types must be strictly identical fails to recognize covariant return types supported since Java 5.

options.text: Compile-time error because secret() in Parent is private, so Child does not override it and @Override is invalid.
Compile-time error because secret cannot be declared public in Child.
No compile error; code runs and prints "Child secret".
Compile-time error because static method secret() cannot be called on instance c.

explanation: Private methods in a superclass are not visible to subclasses and cannot be overridden. In Child, secret() is a distinct new method, causing the @Override annotation to produce a compilation error. The assertion that Child cannot declare secret as public is incorrect, as non-inherited methods may choose any access level.

options.text: Alpha-Object
Beta-String
Beta-String Alpha-Object
Compilation error because Beta does not override test(Object).

explanation: Beta.test(String) overloads, rather than overrides, Alpha.test(Object). The variable a has declared type Alpha, which only exposes test(Object). Therefore, compile-time overload resolution chooses test(Object), and dynamic dispatch calls Alpha's implementation, printing 'Alpha-Object '. The output 'Beta-String ' mistakenly assumes method arguments determine polymorphic dispatch dynamically.

question: Suppose class A declares protected Number calculate(int n). Which of the following signatures in a subclass B extends A is a legal override in Java?

options.text: protected Object calculate(int n)
private Integer calculate(int n)
public Double calculate(long n)
public Integer calculate(int n)

explanation: A valid override must have the identical parameter list (int n), can widen access (protected to public), and can specify a covariant return type (Integer is a subtype of Number). Changing parameter types forms an overload, private reduces visibility illegally, and widening the return type to Object is prohibited.
